# 1 Kings 13 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

The chapter records a dramatic confrontation at Bethel, where an unnamed "man of God" from Judah confronts Jeroboam at his illegitimate altar, delivers a stunning prophecy naming Josiah ~300 years in advance, and then tragically falls through the deception of an old prophet. The central theme is the supremacy and irrevocability of God's word. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-13-commentary; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-13/)

---

## v. 1 — The Man of God Arrives at Bethel

**Traditional Reading:** "By the word of the LORD" renders a Hebrew phrase that literally means "in the word of the LORD." It implies the prophet was not merely commanded to go but was clothed in the inspiration of the word — both the word came *to* him and the Spirit was *upon* him, enabling and compelling him to declare it. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/13.htm)

**Historical Setting:** Jeroboam was standing at the altar to burn incense — likely the inaugural feast of the eighth month he had "devised in his own heart" (1 Kings 12:33). The man of God's arrival was providentially timed for this moment. This was the "final straw" with God: Jeroboam had introduced new worship centers, golden calves, high places with idols, non-Levitical priests, and now he was functioning as a priest himself. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-13-commentary)

**Identity:** Josephus calls the man of God "Jadon" (perhaps Iddo), but Gill notes this cannot be, since Iddo lived long after and chronicled Abijah's reign (2 Chron 13:22). The man of God is deliberately anonymous. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/13.htm)

**Reformed note (Ligonier):** God immediately sent a prophet to confront Jeroboam. The prophet's role was to be a "conservative radical" — calling society *back* to God's law. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/disobedient-prophet)

**"Word of the LORD" concentration:** The phrase appears nine times in this chapter (vv. 1, 2, 5, 9, 17, 18, 20, 26, 32), making it the central theme. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-13-commentary)

---

## v. 2 — The Prophecy Naming Josiah

**Traditional Reading:** The prophet addresses the altar, not Jeroboam — "O altar, altar!" This rhetorical device rebukes Jeroboam's stupidity: the altar is as capable of hearing as he is. The repetition shows the vehemence of the prophet's spirit. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/13.htm)

**The Josiah Prophecy:** Naming Josiah by name ~290-340 years before his birth is one of the most remarkable specific prophecies in Scripture. Ellicott notes that it is on par with the naming of Cyrus in Isaiah 44:28. If one resolves prophecy into mere "intuitive sagacity," this is incredible; if one believes in supernatural foreknowledge, it is simply unusual but not incredible. Ellicott acknowledges some suggest "Josiah by name" might be a later gloss, but argues the name is significant ("one healed by Jehovah") and the particularity is deliberate. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/13.htm)

**Fulfillment:** Recorded in 2 Kings 23:15-20 — Josiah broke down the altar at Bethel, burned human bones upon it to defile it, but spared the tomb of the man of God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-13/)

**Political dimension:** The prophecy that judgment would come through a ruler of the *house of David* (Judah, not Israel) was a special rebuke to Jeroboam, who lived in constant fear of the southern kingdom (cf. 1 Kings 12:27). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-13/)

---

## v. 3 — The Sign Announced

**Traditional Reading:** Because the Josiah prophecy would not be fulfilled for centuries, God graciously provided an *immediate* sign to confirm the word to present-day hearers. Such immediate signs confirming remote prophecies were rare before this period but become more common in later history (cf. 2 Kings 19:29; Isa 7:14-16). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/1-kings-13.html — Barnes)

**Symbolism:** The splitting of the altar and the pouring out of ashes — which according to Levitical law should have been carefully carried to a clean place (Lev 1:16; 4:12; 6:10-11) — symbolized God's utter rejection of this sacrificial system. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-13.html — Constable)

Gill adds: the pouring out of ashes signified not just shaking but complete demolition — the altar would not even be able to retain its ashes. This was "an emblem of the utter abolition of idolatry here in future times." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/13.htm)

---

## vv. 4-5 — The Withered Hand and Split Altar

**Traditional Reading:** Jeroboam stretched out his hand to command the prophet's arrest. The gesture was one of authority. By instantly withering that hand — the very symbol of his power — God demonstrated His superior authority and sovereignty over the king. The king "could not pull it back" — the nerves and muscles shrunk so that his arm remained fixed in its commanding position, a visible emblem of the futility of opposing God's word. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-13.html — Constable; https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/13.htm)

**Three purposes of the withering (Poole, cited by Enduring Word):** (1) to chastise Jeroboam for offering violence to the Lord's prophet; (2) to secure the prophet against further violence; (3) to show how highly God resents injuries done to His ministers faithfully discharging their office. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-13/)

**Ellicott on the signs:** Both signs "shadow forth plainly the thing signified." The shattered altar pictures the coming destruction of Jeroboam's religious system; the withered hand pictures "the miserable failure of his strength and policy when opposed to the Law and the judgment of God." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/13.htm)

---

## v. 6 — Jeroboam's Plea and the Prophet's Intercession

**Traditional Reading:** Jeroboam's tone shifts entirely — from commanding arrest to humble supplication. Yet he calls Yahweh "the LORD *your* God," not "*my* God." This reveals that Jeroboam had no personal relationship with Yahweh; he merely wanted the prophet's God to fix his hand. Wanting something from God is not the same as repentance. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-13/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-13.html — Constable)

The man of God showed remarkable grace — moving instantly from being under arrest to being an intercessor for his persecutor. God answered the prayer and restored the hand, which should have led Jeroboam to repentance. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/13.htm)

**Ellicott:** The withdrawal of this sign of wrath on Jeroboam's submission was "apparently designed to give Jeroboam one more opportunity of repentance." The chapter's closing verses suggest that "but for the interposition of the old prophet of Bethel, he might still have taken that opportunity." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/13.htm)

---

## vv. 7-10 — The Man of God Refuses Jeroboam's Hospitality

**Traditional Reading:** Jeroboam's invitation — "come home with me and refresh yourself, and I will give you a reward" — was an attempt to compromise the prophet. If the prophet accepted the king's hospitality and reward, onlookers would question whether he served Yahweh or Jeroboam. In ancient Near Eastern culture, sharing a meal implied mutual affection and protection. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-13.html — Constable)

**Ellicott explains the prohibition's purpose:** Accepting hospitality would "in the eyes of the people imply a condonation of the idolatrous worship, which might well destroy or extenuate the impression made by the prophet's prediction." It was "evidently to provide against these things — as fatal to the effectiveness of the prophet's mission — that the prohibition of v. 9 was given." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/13.htm)

**The command not to return the same way** was less obvious. Ellicott suggests it meant the prophet should vanish swiftly, like Elisha's messenger to Jehu (2 Kings 9:3, 10), so his route wouldn't be known. "If so, his neglect of the spirit of the command was the first step in the way of his destruction." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/13.htm)

Barnes adds: the refusal to eat or drink was "to show in a marked way, which men generally could appreciate, God's abhorrence of the system which Jeroboam had 'devised of his own heart.'" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/1-kings-13.html — Barnes)

**Reformed application (Ligonier):** The altar prophet initially obeyed God's command not to stay in Bethel. The fulfillment of the altar's destruction (v. 5) confirmed the surety of God's word to him, and Jeroboam offered no sincere repentance that might have warranted a new word. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/disobedient-prophet)

---

## vv. 11-17 — The Old Prophet Pursues the Man of God

**Traditional Reading — Who was the old prophet?** This is a debated question. Ellicott says the narrative "clearly implies" he was "not a mere pretender to prophetic inspiration, nor an apostate from the worship of Jehovah." Rather, like Balaam, "he united true prophetic gifts with a low worldliness of temper, capable on occasion of base subterfuge and deceit." He had thrown in his lot with Jeroboam's policy, yet desired to remain a prophet of the Lord. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/13.htm)

Gill catalogs the ambiguity: "It is hard to say what he was, a good man or a bad man." Evidence against him: dwelling in idolatrous Bethel, allowing his sons to attend idolatrous worship, telling a premeditated lie. Evidence for him: called "an old prophet," did not personally attend the idolatrous worship, showed respect to the man of God, received a true word from God, believed the prophecy, buried the man of God in his own tomb, and wanted to be buried beside him. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/13.htm)

Clarke (cited by Enduring Word): "Probably once a prophet of the Lord, who had fallen from his steadfastness, and yet not so deeply as to lose the knowledge of the true God, and join with Jeroboam with his idolatries." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-13/)

**The oak/terebinth tree:** The man of God was found sitting under "the oak" — a well-known landmark tree, like the oak at Shechem or the palm of Deborah. Ellicott notes this is "an evident mark of the antiquity of the document from which the history is taken." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/13.htm)

**The man of God's second refusal (vv. 16-17):** He repeats the divine command verbatim. He was resolute, though likely hungry and thirsty. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/13.htm)

---

## vv. 18-19 — The Lie and the Fall

**Traditional Reading:** The old prophet's lie was multi-layered: he claimed (1) shared identity ("I too am a prophet as you are"), (2) a spectacular revelation ("an angel spoke to me"), and (3) divine authority ("by the word of the LORD"). The man of God had successfully resisted the king's temptation, but fell to a fellow believer's enticement. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-13/)

**Why the man of God believed the lie (Enduring Word):** Six factors: the old prophet was older and respected; he identified as a fellow prophet; he claimed a spectacular angelic experience; he claimed to speak for the LORD; he didn't seem to be an idolater; he offered only simple food, not a reward. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-13/)

**Ellicott on the culpability:** "The lie was gross, and ought to have been obvious to one who had received a plain command, and must have known that 'God was not a man that He should lie, or the son of man that He should repent.' It was believed, no doubt, because it chimed in with some secret reluctance to obey, and, by obedience, to give up all reward and hospitality. Hence the belief was a self-deceit, and, as such, culpable." Ellicott references Bishop Butler's famous sermon on "Self-deceit." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/13.htm)

**Poole (cited by Enduring Word):** The old prophet's sin was great: "he did not only tell a premeditated lie, but also made God a liar, and to contradict himself, and all this without any pretence of necessity, or benefit to himself." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-13/)

**Desiring God (Vaneetha Rendall Risner):** Uses this passage to illustrate that even trusted people can lead us from the truth: "We can begin to doubt what God has shown us when others question what he's said, or when they offer some fresh 'revelation' or insight that supersedes what God has clearly said… When God's word to us is clear, we need to obey him rather than relying on the opinions of others — even of those we respect." (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-voices-we-hear-in-suffering)

---

## vv. 20-22 — The True Word of Judgment Comes

**Traditional Reading:** The true word of the LORD comes — ironically — through the very lips that had just spoken a lying word. While they sat at the table, the old prophet who had deceived the man of God now becomes the mouthpiece of authentic judgment. Ellicott calls this "perhaps the most terrible feature in the history" — "the Divine sentence is spoken — no doubt, as in the case of Balaam, unwillingly — through the very lips which by falsehood had lured the prophet of Judah from the right path, and at the very table of treacherous hospitality." He sees it as "a symbol of a general law constantly exemplifying itself, that the voice of worldly wisdom first beguiles the servants of God to disobedience by false glosses on their duty to Him, and then proclaims unsparingly their sin and its just punishment." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/13.htm)

**The judgment — no burial in the fathers' tomb:** In the ancient Near East, to be buried away from one's ancestral tomb was a disgrace and a curse. The judgment was precisely proportionate to the sin: he ate and drank where he was told not to, so his body would not reach the place where it belonged. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-13/; citing Wiseman)

**A key theological principle (Enduring Word):** God judged the man of God far more strictly than Jeroboam or the old prophet, though they seemed guilty of worse sins (national idolatry and deliberate lying prophecy). This illustrates 1 Peter 4:17 — judgment begins with the household of God. "God knows that the world will not be reached when His people live in compromise and disobedience." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-13/)

**Clarke (cited by Enduring Word):** "By permitting himself to be seduced by the old prophet, when he should have acted only on the expressly declared counsel of God, he committed the sin unto death [1 John 5:16-17]; that is, such a sin as God will punish with the death of the body, while he extends mercy to his soul." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-13/)

---

## vv. 23-25 — The Lion on the Road

**Traditional Reading:** A lion met and killed the man of God, but then did not eat the body or attack the donkey. The donkey and lion stood beside the corpse — an unmistakably supernatural scene. The lion "seems to be more obedient than the man of God from Judah was" (Enduring Word). The lion acted on a divine commission and did no more than it was appointed to do. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-13/)

Gill: "When the lion had done what he had a commission to do, which was to kill the prophet, he was to do no more." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/13.htm)

**Ellicott on lions in Palestine:** Lions were attested in Palestine until at least the 13th century AD, particularly in southern Palestine and the Jordan valley forests. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/13.htm)

---

## vv. 25-32 — Burial and Testimony

**Traditional Reading — The old prophet's response:** When he hears of the death, the old prophet immediately recognizes it: "It is the man of God who disobeyed the word of the LORD." Ellicott notes "a characteristic reticence as to his own share in the work, in respect both of the deceit and the prediction of judgment, perhaps indicating something of the strange mixture of remorse and unscrupulous policy which comes out in his later action." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/13.htm)

**The burial and mourning:** The old prophet retrieves the body, mourns ("Alas, my brother!"), and buries it in his own tomb — not in the tomb of the man of God's fathers, in fulfillment of the prophecy. Then he instructs his sons to bury him alongside the man of God when he dies. This shows the old prophet genuinely believed the prophecy against the altar at Bethel would come to pass, and he wanted his bones protected from the coming desecration Josiah would bring. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-13/; https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/13.htm)

**Ellicott on the mixed motives:** The mourning and burial "probably show some touch of remorse and personal compassion for the victim of his treacherous policy, mingled with the desire of preserving the tomb, which was to be his own last resting-place, from desecration, when the prediction of the prophet of Judah should be accomplished." He adds that the old prophet's policy succeeded: "The messenger of wrath had been enticed to familiar intercourse with the prophet of the new idolatry, and had been publicly proclaimed as his 'brother': probably his death had been used to discredit his warning. The result is seen in the significant notice of v. 33: 'After this thing, Jeroboam returned not from his evil way.' Hence the seriousness of the disobedience, which played into the hands of wickedness, and the startling severity of the penalty." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/13.htm)

**Fulfillment confirmed:** When Josiah later destroyed the altar (2 Kings 23:15-20), he saw the tomb of the man of God and ordered it left undisturbed, sparing also the bones of the old prophet buried beside him. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-13-commentary)

**Trapp:** "All these wonderful accidents, as God's hammers, did but beat upon cold iron." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-13/)

---

## vv. 33-34 — Jeroboam's Unrepentance

**Traditional Reading:** Despite everything — the withering and restoration of his hand, the splitting altar, the death of the man of God — Jeroboam did not repent. He continued appointing non-Levitical priests from every class of people. The phrase "whoever wished, he consecrated him" (v. 33) possibly indicates that, despite all Jeroboam's efforts, there was "some difficulty in securing candidates for his unauthorised priesthood." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/13.htm)

**Enduring Word:** Jeroboam "had great opportunity" given the promise in 1 Kings 11:38 ("if you heed all that I command you… I will build for you an enduring house"), but he never fulfilled his potential. He became the prototype of disobedient kings — the phrase "walked in the way of Jeroboam, and in his sin by which he had made Israel sin" is used of at least twelve subsequent northern kings. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-13/)

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### Reformed / Ligonier
Emphasizes God's sovereignty over the word and the principle that God does not contradict Himself. The altar prophet died because "we cannot believe a new 'word from God'… when it violates what God has already spoken." Application to the new covenant era: "We must test everything by what God has said, believing only what is in conformity with the written Word of God." This is tied to *sola Scriptura* — the written Word is the final authority. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/disobedient-prophet)

### Baptist / Desiring God (John Piper tradition)
The Desiring God article uses 1 Kings 13 to illustrate the danger of listening to competing voices rather than God's clear word — especially in suffering. The point is pastoral and experiential: when God's word is clear, obey it rather than relying on the opinions of others, even trusted spiritual leaders. The article ties this to the sufficiency of Scripture: "Scripture attunes our ears to what his voice sounds like… God will never contradict what he's told us in the Bible." (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-voices-we-hear-in-suffering)

## Other Views

*Within the search and fetch limits, I was unable to retrieve dedicated Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com), Orthodox (oca.org), or modern scholarly (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org) treatments of this chapter. What follows is drawn from sites within the permitted list that address certain critical questions.*

### The "Later Date" Question (Pulpit Commentary)
Some commentators consider this chapter to derive from a different source than the surrounding narratives. The expression "the cities of Samaria" in v. 32 is cited as evidence of later composition, since Samaria wasn't built as a capital until Omri's reign (~880 BC). The style and "colouring" of the story suggest it "embodies a tradition current in the time of the compiler." The Pulpit Commentary, however, treats the chapter as describing events of Jeroboam's inaugural feast. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-13.html)

### The "Josiah by Name" Debate
Ellicott acknowledges some scholars suggest "Josiah by name" may be "a marginal gloss which has crept into the text, or the insertion of the chronicler writing after the event." He argues against this, noting the name's significance ("one healed by Jehovah") and comparing it to Cyrus in Isaiah 44:28. The credibility of such particularity depends on one's view of prophetic inspiration: naturalistic "intuitive sagacity" vs. supernatural access to "the mind of God." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/13.htm)

### Josephus's Tradition
Josephus (Antiquities 8.9) names the man of God "Jadon" and provides additional traditions about the old prophet's attempts to remove any impression made on Jeroboam's mind. Ellicott dismisses identifying him with Iddo, since Iddo chronicled Abijah's reign and lived much later. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_kings/13.htm)
